$comment: Shared dynamic-route-segment syntax table.
Two halves in two languages decide what a dynamic route segment is, and they
are not allowed to disagree:
- crates/ruvyxa_graph/src/lib.rs  (route_segment / validate_dynamic_name)
decides which app/ folder names become routes at all, and writes the
surviving pattern into the manifest.
- packages/@ruvyxa/core/src/route-match.ts  (compilePattern) decides which
manifest segments compile to a parameter capture. A segment it does not
recognise becomes a *literal* URL component.
When discovery accepts a name the matcher does not recognise, the route is
written into the manifest, shows up in the route table, passes `ruvyxa check`
— and never matches a request, because the only URL that would match is the
literal folder name. Nothing reports it: each half believes it is right.
That was RUV-H20, found with `app/blog/[post-id]/page.tsx`.
The rule this file pins is one rule: a parameter name is one or more ASCII
letters, digits, or `_` — exactly JavaScript's `\w` without the `u` flag,
which is what compilePattern already matched. Discovery was narrowed to it.
The invariant every case encodes: for a bracketed segment, discovery accepts
it if and only if the matcher compiles it to a parameter.
Every implementation replays this file:
- crates/ruvyxa_graph/src/lib.rs  (replays_the_shared_route_pattern_conformance_table)
- tests/packages/core/route-pattern-conformance.test.ts
Add a case here first when changing segment syntax; a port that drifts then
fails in the language that drifted, not in review.
$kindComment: kind is what the JavaScript matcher must produce for the segment:
static             — no capture; the segment is a literal URL component
dynamic            — one capture, one path segment              [name]
catchAll           — one capture, one or more path segments     [...name]
optionalCatchAll   — one capture, zero or more path segments    [[...name]]
rejected           — route discovery refuses the folder (RUV1002)
`param` is the parameter name the matcher must bind, or null when there is
none. A `rejected` case also asserts the matcher would NOT have bound a
parameter — that is precisely why the name has to be refused at build time
rather than allowed through to a silent 404.
Every case is replayed as the final segment of a route, so a catch-all is
never in the position that would trip the separate 'catch-all must be last'

segments.why: Control: an ordinary folder is a literal URL component in both halves.
A static segment carries any character. Only parameter *names* are restricted.
The common case, and the one every template ships.
camelCase is the shape the framework recommends, since params.postId has to be writable.
Underscore is inside \w, so both halves have always agreed on it.
Digits are inside \w.
\w allows a leading digit. Not an identifier, but params['2'] is a usable key and neither half is confused by it — the rule is the character set, not JavaScript identifier syntax.
Catch-all names go through the same validation as [name].
Optional catch-all names go through the same validation as [name].

RUV-H20 itself. Discovery accepted a hyphen; compilePattern's \w does not, so /blog/[post-id] compiled to a literal and /blog/hello 404'd on every host. A hyphenated name is also unwritable as params.post-id.
The same hyphen in a catch-all: ^\[\.\.\.(\w+)\]$ fails it just the same.
The same hyphen in an optional catch-all.
A dot was accepted anywhere but the first character. It is outside \w, so the matcher read the whole segment as a literal.
`$` is a legal JavaScript identifier character but is outside \w, which is the character set the matcher actually implements. The matcher is the authority here.
A space in a folder name was accepted by discovery and never matched.
JavaScript's \w without the `u` flag is ASCII-only, so a non-ASCII name is a literal to the matcher however valid an identifier it is.
Empty name. Refused before and after; the matcher would have read it as the literal segment `[]`.
Empty catch-all name.
Empty optional catch-all name.
A leading dot was already refused, to keep [.foo] from reading as a mangled catch-all.
Unbalanced brackets: the name would be `[...slug`, which still contains a bracket.
Unbalanced the other way; the name would be `slug]`.
A bracket outside the [name] forms is refused outright rather than becoming a literal segment with brackets in the URL.
